itemOffered.name: Criminal Appeals
itemOffered.description: A criminal appeal challenges a conviction or a sentence after the case has been decided. Appeals from the Magistrates' Court go to the Crown Court, and appeals from the Crown Court go to the Court of Appeal. The time to appeal is short and starts on the day of the decision.

itemOffered.description: Advice on the prospects of appealing a conviction or sentence, including review of transcript, summing-up, and trial papers.

itemOffered.name: Drafting Grounds of Appeal
itemOffered.description: Drafting of grounds of appeal for conviction and sentence appeals.

itemOffered.name: Crown Court Appeals from the Magistrates' Court

itemOffered.name: Court of Appeal (Criminal Division)
itemOffered.description: Representation in the Court of Appeal (Criminal Division) for conviction and sentence appeals.

mainEntity.name: How long do I have to appeal a criminal conviction or sentence?

acceptedAnswer.text: Time limits are short and start running on the day of the decision. Call before the time runs — grounds can be drafted in time even if the papers are not yet available.

mainEntity.name: Can I appeal just the sentence rather than the conviction?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. Sentence-only appeals are common. Grounds depend on the principles applied and the facts. The first call covers whether they are realistic.

mainEntity.name: My trial lawyer said an appeal is not worth it — is that final?

acceptedAnswer.text: No. A second opinion on prospects is part of the work. The first call covers whether the case is worth pursuing.
